title: Errors in a billing tool
excerpt: When an invoice fails, say what broke and whether it was sent. An error code and a sad illustration waste the moment money is in question.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, the moment a decision becomes a mark on the page.
caption: A person signing a paper document, a decision put in ink. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a billing error say first?
faqs.answer: Say whether the invoice was sent, and to whom, before you explain the cause. A finance lead who is afraid of a wrong invoice is asking that question already. 'Not sent' or 'Sent to ap@acme.com' is the first line. The reason and the next action come immediately after.

faqs.question: Should retry be the default?
faqs.answer: Only when retry cannot double-charge or double-send. If the invoice might have gone out, the default is to check status, not to fire it again. A blind Try again button is how duplicates are born. Name the safe action instead.

faqs.question: Where do error codes belong?
faqs.answer: Behind the sentence, for support, not instead of the sentence. The lead should know what to do without reading a code. If the only path to understanding is a code, the error state is unfinished.

markdown:
Billing tool error states should answer the fear first: was the invoice sent, and what should happen next. The finance lead who is afraid of a wrong invoice does not need a code, and they do not need a sad illustration. They need to know whether money, or a request for money, has left the building.

Until that is clear, every other word is noise.

## Was it sent

The first sentence is a status, not an apology. "Not sent. Acme was not emailed." Or: "Sent to ap@acme.com at 4:02 p.m. Central. The payment itself failed afterward." Those are different emergencies. Mixing them into "something went wrong" forces the lead to check the customer's inbox, which is the moment they stop trusting the tool.

If you are unsure whether it sent, say you are unsure, and say what you are doing to resolve it. Uncertainty with a next step is acceptable. False certainty is not. "Probably not sent" is worse than "We cannot confirm yet. Do not retry. We will show the status on this invoice." A retry from an unknown state is how a customer receives two invoices and forwards both to their finance team with a question you did not want asked.

Put this sentence on the invoice, not only in a toast. Toasts vanish. The lead will turn to a colleague and the toast will be gone, and the argument about what happened will begin. The invoice's status line is the record. Make the error the status, until it is resolved. Keep the amount and the recipient visible beside it so the failure stays attached to the right object. An error page that forgets which invoice it belongs to is a second failure.

[The WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) organizes the standard under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, and it covers web applications. A billing error has to be understandable in text and operable as a next step. Color, a red icon, or a shaking field is not the message. The message is a sentence. It has to be in the page, available to a screen reader, and still there after the lead looks away to find a purchase order. WCAG is the floor. The fear of a wrong invoice is the reason to go beyond the floor and be painfully plain.

## What broke, in ledger language

After status, the cause, in words they already use.

Tax was not calculated, so send was blocked. Say which line is missing a rate. Currency does not match the customer's last paid invoice. Say both currencies. The number collides with an invoice that already exists. Show the other number and the date. The payment method was declined. Say the decline in human speech, "the card was declined," and whether a retry will create a second invoice. The email bounced. Say the address. The total does not match the sum of the lines. Show the two numbers. Do not make them export a CSV to learn why you refused.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) treats topics that affect financial stability as places where trust matters more, not less. A cute error is a trust error. So is a vague one. The lead should be able to forward your sentence to their own customer, or to their accountant, without translating it. "Invoice 1044 was not sent because tax was missing on the second line" can be forwarded. "Error BIL-17" cannot. Write the forwardable sentence. Put the code in a detail disclosure for the person who files a bug.

Do not blame the customer, and do not blame "the user," who is your lead. "Invalid customer" is a slur against a record you stored. "This customer has no email on file" is a fact and a fix. The fix belongs in the same view: add the email, then return to the unsent invoice with the amount unchanged. Do not dump them into a customer editor that forgets the draft.

## The next action is specific

Offer the safe action as the primary button. "Save as draft" when send is blocked. "Add the tax rate" when that is the block. "View the other invoice" when the number collided. "Mark the email corrected and send once" only when you know the first send did not happen.

Retry is allowed when the failure was a timeout and you have idempotency, which is a product property you must actually have. If pressing the button twice can send two invoices or capture two payments, the button must not say "Try again." It must say the safer thing, even if engineering would prefer a simple retry. The interface is not allowed to be braver than the ledger.

If a partial success happened, split it in the first two lines, not in a paragraph. "The invoice email was sent. The card was not charged." Then tell them whether they should wait, send a different kind of note, or collect payment another way. Partial success that looks like failure produces a second send. Partial success that looks like full success produces a polite customer and a missing payment. Both are expensive. The copy is cheap.

Void and credit are not error buttons by default. They are how a panicked lead tries to undo a send that actually failed to send, and then the books get stranger. Only offer void when the invoice exists and void is the intent. If it was never sent, "discard draft" is the undo. Use different words so muscle memory cannot void a real invoice while trying to drop a draft.

## No illustration, no joke, no code as the headline

An illustration of a broken piggy bank, a sad receipt, or a disconnected plug spends the moment on metaphor. The lead already understands that something failed. The metaphor does not say whether Acme was emailed. Cut it. Use the space for the recipient, the amount, and the button.

A joke is worse on this screen than almost anywhere else in the product. The person is imagining a customer on the phone. A quip from the software is a colleague who does not understand the room. Be quiet and specific. You can be warm without being funny. "The invoice is still a draft. Nothing was emailed." is warm enough.

Codes as headlines push the lead into a help center during the worst minute. Help centers are for setup. This minute is for containment. If support needs the code, they can open details, or the lead can copy a single "copy details" control that includes the code, the invoice id, and the time. Do not make them read the code aloud off a giant type treatment you thought looked technical and reassuring. It looks like a crash.

Banners that say "there was a problem with one or more invoices" above a list, without marking which rows, are a scavenger hunt. Mark the row. Repeat the short status in the row. The lead should not open twenty invoices to find the one you refused to name.

## Failures that must not look like success

The dangerous visual is a green state that appears before the ledger agrees. A checkmark on tap, then a failure a second later, trains people to walk away at the checkmark. Wait to confirm. If the send is slow, show "Sending… not confirmed" rather than an optimistic success. When the result arrives, replace it with the truth. Never leave the optimistic state up because the request timed out. Timeout is "not confirmed," and the next screen is the status check, not a celebration.

Email and payment are separate confirmations. Do not use one checkmark for both. A lead who sees "done" will tell a customer "you should have it," and the customer will not have it, or will have the email and not the charge. Split the receipts. Two lines, two words, both plain.

Scheduled sends fail in the future, when the lead is gone. The error has to survive until they return: a status on the first screen, not an email alone, and not a notification they muted. "Scheduled send did not go out" is the object when they next open the tool. Do not clear it because a newer draft exists. The failed schedule is the older fear and the more important one.

Duplicates need a comparison, not a string. "This looks like invoice 1039, sent yesterday, for the same amount to the same email." Show both. Let them open the older one. The action is "keep this as draft" unless they explicitly choose to send a second. Default to not sending. The fear is the product's ally if you let it be.

## A review of the money errors

List every way send, charge, void, and schedule can fail. For each, write: was it sent, what broke, what to press. Read them aloud to someone who did not build the ledger. If they ask a question your text does not answer, add the answer, do not add a drawing. Time the recovery. The lead should know whether to contact the customer within a minute.

Test the unclear middle: kill the network after the tap. The UI must land on "not confirmed," with the invoice identifiable, and with retry absent unless it is safe. This is the test teams skip because it is annoying to stage. It is also the production incident.

Then read the same states in a screen reader and at larger text. If the status only exists as a color on the total, it is invisible to some of the people responsible for the books. The sentence is the feature.

Permissions decide who is even allowed to press send, and a forbidden send should not look like a ledger failure. [Permissions in a billing tool](/blog/permissions-in-a-billing-tool) is the next piece, because the lead needs to see what they can issue, what they can only draft, and why a control is locked before they ever hit an error.

[Selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) shows the standard of interface Hanabi designs and builds: clear hierarchy, and language that says what happens next.
